title: Australian household security is being stretched across housing, food, work fit, and life-course timing while intimate relationships remain a resilient resource
source_unit: Melbourne Institute of Applied Economic and Social Research, University of Melbourne, 2026 HILDA Annual Statistical Report
geography: Australia; nationally representative HILDA household panel, Waves 1–24 with selected 2024 outcomes

observations.period: 2001–2024 HILDA panel; education, work fit, and life-course timing

denominator.unit: approximately Australians followed annually in the HILDA panel

overeducation.unit: approximately half of Australian workers described as over-educated for their job in the 2026 report summary

young_adults_at_home.unit: approximately half of Australians aged 18–29 living with parents in the report summary

life_course_compression.value: education, job fit, housing independence and household formation are interacting rather than moving as separate transitions

observations.method: Annual HILDA Statistical Report synthesis of longitudinal household-panel data collected from 2001 through 2024; the public university summary reports headline findings while detailed estimates and definitions remain in the full report.
observations.uncertainty: The public summary does not provide every denominator, subgroup estimate, or model specification for the headline findings; over-education and living-at-home measures require the report’s precise definitions and should not be treated as causal effects.
observations.subgroup: Australian workers, young adults aged 18–29, and HILDA household members followed over time.
observations.counterinterpretation: Living with parents may reflect preference, cultural norms, education, care exchange, or housing-market conditions; over-education can reflect career entry, changing skill requirements, or worker choice.

observations.period: 2024 HILDA outcome; food insecurity and household security

denominator.unit: approximately Australians followed annually in the HILDA panel; exact food-insecurity analytic denominator is report-specific

food_insecurity.value: more than one in six Australians aged 15 and over

economic_pressure.value: employment remains high while housing and money stress increase

security_conversion.value: employment does not automatically convert into food, housing, or financial security

observations.method: HILDA longitudinal panel analysis summarized in the 2026 Annual Statistical Report; the report covers selected waves and 2024 outcomes across economic wellbeing, housing, food insecurity and related domains.
observations.uncertainty: The public university summary does not publish the full food-insecurity instrument, weighting details, duration measure, or causal decomposition; the reported share is not a food-bank use or nutritional-health outcome.
observations.subgroup: Australians aged 15 and over and households observed through HILDA’s annual panel.
observations.counterinterpretation: Food insecurity can be episodic, seasonal, or buffered by informal support; employment status alone does not identify income adequacy, food access, or household coping.

observations.period: 2001–2024 HILDA panel; family relationship quality and household resilience

denominator.unit: approximately Australians followed annually in the HILDA panel; relationship analytic samples vary by wave

partner_relationships.value: life-partner relationships are reported as very strong

resilience_counterweight.value: strong intimate relationships coexist with financial, housing, food and work stress

social_infrastructure_boundary.value: household and intimate relationships may buffer insecurity without removing structural constraints

observations.method: HILDA repeated annual interviews tracking household and family relationships, economic wellbeing, employment, health and subjective wellbeing over more than two decades.
observations.uncertainty: The public summary does not establish whether relationship quality causes resilience or how relationship measures interact with income, housing, care, or health trajectories at the individual level.
observations.subgroup: Australian partnered and household respondents across HILDA waves.
observations.counterinterpretation: Strong relationship ratings can reflect selection, adaptation, reporting norms, or survivorship; they do not imply equal access to supportive relationships or absence of household conflict.

observations.period: 2001–2024 HILDA panel; wellbeing and fatigue by age

denominator.unit: approximately Australians followed annually in the HILDA panel; age-specific analytic samples vary

younger_health.value: younger people report worse health in the 2026 report summary

time_health_route.value: economic and household pressure is accompanied by wellbeing and fatigue signals, not only financial measures

observations.method: Longitudinal HILDA analysis summarized across annual waves and selected 2024 health and wellbeing outcomes.
observations.uncertainty: The public summary does not specify the health instrument, fatigue measure, age cut points, or causal pathway; reported health is not clinical diagnosis or medical utilization.
observations.subgroup: Australian respondents across age groups, with emphasis on younger people in the report summary.
observations.counterinterpretation: Age differences may reflect reporting, cohort, labor-market, housing, family, or survey-period effects rather than a single national fatigue cause.

related_sources.claim: Official HILDA overview documents the nationally representative household panel, annual follow-up, and long-run scope.
Australian Government Department of Social Services describes HILDA governance, coverage and data access.

boundary: This record adds a comparative longitudinal household-security route: life-course timing, job fit, food insecurity, housing and financial stress, intimate relationships, fatigue and age-linked wellbeing should be read together without assuming that employment or relationship strength automatically produces security. It is an official report synthesis of HILDA panel evidence, not a new respondent-level extraction or causal evaluation.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official University of Melbourne summary, HILDA report index, and HILDA study overview were browser-reviewed for the 2026 report scope, Waves 1–24 coverage, panel scale, over-education, food insecurity, living-at-home, relationships, financial/housing stress, fatigue and younger-health findings. The report PDF was not shell-retrievable because the host returned 403/content-length access errors; URL fingerprints are retained for the accessible official pages.
